summary: Extends the Network Services Monitoring MIB from RFC 2788 to define objects for monitoring mail transfer agents. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: It is a dashboard for mail servers that shows how much mail they are handling.

questions: how to monitor an mta with snmp
what is the mail monitoring mib
subtitle: SNMP objects that let a management system watch message flow, queues and errors inside a mail server.

tldr.problem: Operators who run Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) had no standard way to see how much mail each one received, stored and sent, or what errors it hit.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB extends the Network Services Monitoring MIB with counters and gauges per MTA, plus a table of per-group statistics, a table linking associations to groups, and a table of errors keyed by status code.
tldr.outcome: It gives a common SNMP view of MTAs, including those inside gateways. RFC 2789 obsoletes RFC 2249 and RFC 1566 and corrects technical errors in them.

today: RFC 2789 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2000. It obsoletes RFC 2249 and RFC 1566, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Mail Monitoring MIB Is
sections.content:
RFC 2789 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) used by Internet network management protocols. It extends the basic Network Services Monitoring MIB from RFC 2788 so that Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) can be monitored. It may also be used for MTA components inside gateways.

The module is written in SMIv2. The RFC explains that an SMIv1 version can be produced by translation, which must stay semantically equivalent except for objects that cannot be translated (those using Counter64).

If a host has one or more MTAs, any number of them may be monitored. Each MTA is treated as a separate network service with its own applTable entry in the Network Services Monitoring MIB. The document covers only the MTA-specific part.
sections.eli5: It is a standard way for a control room to ask a mail server, "how are you doing?" and get answers in a form every tool understands.

sections.title: The Message Flow Model
sections.content:
The MIB rests on a model in which a message passes through four steps inside an MTA:

  1. The MTA receives the message from a User Agent, Message Store, another MTA or a gateway.
  2. The "next hop" is determined. A message can have several next hops, which may require duplicating it.
  3. If necessary, the message is converted into the format the next hop needs. Conversion may succeed or fail.
  4. The message is transmitted to its destination.

Storage happens at some point, but different MTAs store at different points. Some expand messages into copies on arrival, so steps 1 to 3 happen before storage. Others store messages as received and do everything during retransmission. As a result, the count of messages received may not equal messages stored, and stored may not equal retransmitted.
sections.eli5: A letter arrives, the clerk decides where it goes next, maybe puts it in a different envelope, and sends it on. Different post offices put the letter on a shelf at different moments, so their counts will not always match.

sections.title: The Four Tables
sections.content:
The MIB defines four tables. The first, mtaTable, holds per-MTA information that is not specific to any part of the MTA. The second, mtaGroupTable, breaks each MTA into separate components called groups. The third, mtaGroupAssociationTable, correlates associations tracked by the network services MIB with groups in different MTAs. The fourth, mtaGroupErrorTable, tracks errors encountered during operation.

The first two tables must be implemented to conform. The last two are optional.

mtaTable is indexed by applIndex and has 12 objects, such as mtaReceivedMessages, mtaStoredMessages and mtaTransmittedMessages, with matching volume (in K-octets) and recipient counts, converted-message counters and mtaLoopsDetected. Received and transmitted values are Counter32. Stored values are Gauge32.
sections.eli5: There are four sheets. One has totals for the whole mail server, one has totals for each of its sections, and two optional sheets track open connections and mistakes.

sections.title: Groups, Associations and Errors
sections.content:
MTAs usually separate inbound reception, queue storage and outbound transmission in some way. The MIB calls such a breakdown a group. It is not the same as an SNMP group, and the term "channel" is avoided because an MTA need not map its channels one-to-one onto groups. Groups may overlap, so summing group values may not equal the mtaTable values, and mtaTable should always be accurate for the MTA as a whole.

Groups can be created at any time after MTA initialization. Once created, a group should not be deleted, and its mtaGroupIndex should not change, unless the MTA is reinitialized. This lets monitoring agents rely on group assignments across queries. Counters a group does not use must be inaccessible, for example returning noSuchName in SNMPv1 or noSuchInstance in SNMPv2. The mtaGroupHierarchy object shows how groups nest: a positive value is the index of a group that includes this one, a negative value is a group collection code, and zero means hierarchy is not implemented.

Each group entry holds message, volume and recipient counters, the age of the oldest stored message, inbound and outbound association counts, last-activity times, failure reasons, the scheduled retry time, the mail protocol in use, a name, a description and a URL. The failure-reason objects should read never if no attempt has been made since initialization.

In the error table, mtaStatusCode encodes an Enhanced Mail System Status Code from RFC 1893 of the form class.subject.detail. The index is ((class * 1000) + subject) * 1000 + detail, with class 2, 4 or 5. Each entry counts inbound, internal and outbound errors.
sections.eli5: Each section of the post office keeps its own tally of letters, connections, and problems. Mistakes are filed under a code number so you can see which kind happened most.

sections.title: Compliance and Changes Since RFC 2249
sections.content:
The module defines compliance statements for implementations of RFC 1566, RFC 2249 and RFC 2789, each with a basic, an association, an error and a full variant where applicable. Object groups such as mtaRFC2789Group list which objects are required.

This revision fixes technical errors in RFC 2249. It changes all DisplayStrings to SnmpAdminStrings, corrects the conformance groups for the different versions, adds the required mtaStatusCode entry to MtaGroupErrorEntry (which does not affect the bits on the wire), and removes the recommendation to return an empty string after a successful operation from mtaGroupInboundRejectionReason and mtaGroupOutboundConnectFailureReason, since it conflicted with their purpose. The module notes that the DisplayString change is not strictly supported by SMIv2, but deprecating and redefining objects would hurt compatibility more.

The module's revision history also records that the original version was published in RFC 1566, and that RFC 2249 added group descriptions and URLs, conversion counters, hierarchy, specific error counters, oldest message IDs, loop counters and the error table.
sections.eli5: This version is a cleanup of an older one. It fixes small mistakes and says exactly which sets of scoreboard items a server must support.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If it is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through SNMP SET operations.

The MIB does expose passive information about the existence, type and configuration of applications on a host, which could hint at vulnerabilities, and about network usage, which could be used to analyze traffic patterns. SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and even a secure network gives no control over who may access the objects. Implementers are encouraged to consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2574 and RFC 2575). The user is responsible for configuring the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals have access.
sections.eli5: The scoreboard is look-only, so nobody can change the numbers. But the numbers could still tell a snoop how busy you are, so you should lock the door to who can read them.
